As President Donald Trump campaigned for the nation's highest office in 2024, he regularly blamed Democrats for the country's economic anxiety.
During campaign stops across the U.S., Trump frequently asked voters if they were better off than they were four years prior. At the time, his message appeared to land: In an election centered on inflation and the cost of living, Trump won every swing state and the nationwide popular vote.
Two years later, voters grappling with those same kitchen-table issues took away much of his party's power in Washington and in states across the country.
Democrats rode a blue wave of historic proportions in Tuesday's midterm election to flip everything from battleground congressional seats to long-held Republican governorships. The Democratic Party will now have control of both the House and Senate, ending the Republican Party's trifecta of power in the federal government.
Nearly nine out of 10 voters in the CNBC Voter Poll said the cost of living was a crucial or major factor in their vote for Congress. Participants in the poll ranked the economy as the most important issue facing the country during the midterm election, ahead of topics like the state of democracy and immigration. Three out of every four survey participants rated the economy as "poor" or "not so good," compared with just 2% who described it as "excellent."
And perhaps most telling of all: Fewer than one out of every five voters said their family's financial standing was better than it was two years ago.
Much of their dissatisfaction was centered on Trump himself, with about two out of every three voters saying his policies worsened economic conditions in the country.
"It was all about the economy," said Mark Zandi, chief economist at Moody's Analytics. "Most Americans are struggling with the high inflation and have been for quite some time, and they're just angry."
A 'breaking point'
Tuesday's election played out against the backdrop of a war with Iran that has been politically unpopular and exacerbated the inflationary pressures facing everyday Americans. The CNBC Voter Poll found nearly three out of every four people said the war was a crucial or major factor in their vote for Congress.
Trump told Fox News that voters were presumably unhappy with the surge in gas prices, even if they generally agreed with the need for military action against Iran. Vice President JD Vance said on social media that some voters who backed him and Trump in 2024 likely supported Democrats in the midterms as a result of the war.
U.S. drivers paid about $4.15 for an average gallon of gas on Tuesday, the highest of any midterm or presidential election day since at least 2000, according to AAA. Gas prices have surged about 37% over the past year as the Middle East conflict crippled the global crude trade.
"America sent a very clear message," said Patrick De Haan, head of petroleum analysis at GasBuddy, a fuel price tracking platform. "Going into an election with prices that on Election Day have never been higher is something that garners a lot of frustration from consumers."
Higher prices for gas and other energy products have cost the average American household nearly $1,230 since the start of the Iran war, according to an analysis from Zandi. Two weeks out from my first marathon, I looked in the mirror and didn’t see the version of myself I thought I would. There was no six-pack, not even a hint of ab definition. My glutes weren’t particularly sculpted, and I wouldn’t exactly describe myself as lean like many runners I see.
At 5-foot-10, I’ve never been the smallest girl in the room. And while my long legs certainly help me cover more distance, I expected months of marathon training to leave me looking more visibly athletic, with more muscle definition and a physique that reflected just how hard I’d been working. I thought that after months of early alarms, added protein, and steadily increasing mileage, I’d look in the mirror and see a different body type.
Somewhere along the way, I absorbed the idea that a runner’s body should look a certain way. When mine didn’t match that image, I started wondering if I wasn’t training hard enough, if I was doing something wrong, or if my body simply wasn’t responding the way it was supposed to.
As I approached race day, I thought about why I was holding myself to that standard in the first place, especially because I was running the New York City Marathon on behalf of Planned Parenthood of Greater New York, an organization whose work centers on bodily autonomy and compassionate care.
Why was I putting so much pressure on my body to look different when it was already doing something incredible? I realized training for a marathon isn’t just about building endurance; it can also mean confronting the expectations you place on yourself.
Where Does the Idea of a ‘Runner’s Body’ Come From?
So many people have an idea of what a “runner’s body” is supposed to look like, particularly fed by what we see online. When you see the same body type represented over and over, it’s easy to start associating that appearance with athleticism. But running a marathon is an enormous physical undertaking, and there’s no single body type that proves you’re capable of doing it.
Clinical sport psychologist Hillary Cauthen, PsyD, explains that the concept of “a runner’s body” is “largely a socially constructed ideal influenced by media representation, sport culture, and the tendency to associate certain physical characteristics with athletic success.” She adds that distance running has historically been represented by a lean body type, particularly smaller-framed athletes, which can leave some recreational runners questioning whether they fit the mold.
Comparison is a large part of this problem, too, says Cindra Kamphoff, PhD, mental performance coach and founder of the Mentally Strong Institute. “We see elite runners and start believing that’s what we should look like,” she explains.
Marathon training is practically a master class in comparison, making it hard to avoid. You’re tracking your pace, watching your mileage climb, sharing runs on Strava, and seeing what everyone else is doing. It can feel like your body should be changing right alongside your stats.
There’s also a particularly frustrating point of tension for women, who can feel caught between the cultural expectation to be smaller and the athletic ideal of looking lean and strong. One CNBC trader says the fever has broken in energy and oil won't see $100 again. A rival panelist warns of a black swan that could flip the trade overnight, and income investors holding Exxon and Chevron have the most…

Joe Terranova made a direct call on oil on CNBC’s Halftime Report on Wednesday, the morning after Democrats swept the midterm elections: “I think that inflation lost last night. I think inflation lost and we’re seeing it reflected today in the price of energy. I think the fever has broken in the energy trade. I would be very surprised to see oil spike back up to $100.”
Energy has led the market for most of 2026. If Terranova is right, the main force behind that run is fading.
Why Terranova Thinks the Energy Fever Broke
His argument goes like this. Oil has carried a war premium for months because of the U.S. conflict with Iran. The Wall Street Journal reported that oil futures fell Wednesday after the Democratic sweep of Congress raised market expectations for a quick settlement to the Middle East conflict. Vice President JD Vance linked his party’s losses to the conflict, posting “The reason we lost is the war.” Take away the war premium, and you take away one of the biggest inputs to inflation.
How Oil and Energy Stocks Traded Into the Vote
Oil had already started falling before polls closed. WTI crude spot prices peaked at $110.01 on October 19, then slid from $107.56 on October 30 to $99.64 on November 3, down $3.73 from a week earlier.
Energy stocks fell along with oil. The Energy Select Sector SPDR Fund (NYSEARCA:XLE) dropped 7.1% over the past week to $63.59. It is still up 45.04% year to date. Exxon Mobil (NYSE:XOM | XOM Price Prediction) lost 7.65% on the week to $169.27 and remains up 40.66% for 2026. Chevron (NYSE:CVX) fell 6.26% to $216.96, which still leaves it up 42.35% this year. So far the pullback has taken back only a small part of the year’s gains.
What Could Prove Him Wrong
Oil can spike quickly. WTI went from $85.23 on September 25 to $99.37 on September 28. It also closed at $100.06 just two sessions before Terranova spoke.
Steve Weiss pushed back on the same show: “I think there’s more than a reasonable probability that Trump does something aggressive with Iran so he can call that a victory, which he’s in sorely need of. That puts a damper on the inflation story, the rate story. A black swan event that’s likely to happen.”
Supply policy is the other risk. OPEC+ agreed to keep November production targets steady and indicated that more changes are unlikely before next year. If peace talks stall, producers have shown no rush to add barrels.

Adobe (NASDAQ:ADBE) came under fresh pressure Wednesday after Citi downgraded the stock to Sell from Neutral and cut its price target to $207 from $250, warning that consensus expectations for fiscal 2027 may still be too high.
Citi sees a rising risk of what it called a hard reset as incoming CEO Anil Chakravarthy takes over on December 1 amid important leadership vacancies, including the CFO and head of Digital Media. The bank expects those changes, combined with a shifting Creative strategy, could lead to a weaker fiscal 2027 outlook when Adobe reports fourth-quarter results.
The strategic shift is important.
Adobe is increasingly prioritizing user growth through AI products such as Firefly rather than relying as heavily on Creative Cloud price increases. Citi believes that could help expand Adobe's funnel over time, but it may hurt annual recurring revenue growth in the near term as more users enter through lower-priced products.
The bank estimates that this strategy could create roughly 200 basis points of pressure on fiscal 2027 ARR growth, with another 50-basis-point headwind as Adobe laps previous Creative Cloud pricing increases. Citi also cited weak small-business demand and growing competition from web-based and AI-native creative tools.
As a result, Citi cut its net new ARR estimates for fiscal 2027 and 2028 by roughly $470 million and $500 million, respectively. It now expects total ARR growth of about 5.3% in fiscal 2027 and 4.5% in fiscal 2028, roughly 200 to 300 basis points below Wall Street expectations.
Margins could face pressure too.
Citi lowered its fiscal 2027 non-GAAP gross-margin estimate by 70 basis points, partly reflecting AI inference costs that Adobe has not yet fully monetized.
Investor Takeaway
I think Citi's call gets to the heart of Adobe's problem.
The company is not necessarily losing the AI race, but the economics of adapting to it may be worse before they get better.
Adobe wants more users, more Firefly adoption, and stronger positioning against AI-native rivals. But if that means fewer price increases, lower-priced entry products, and higher inference costs, near-term ARR growth and margins could weaken at exactly the wrong time.
That is what Citi means by a hard reset.
For investors, the key things to watch are Adobe's fiscal 2027 guidance, Creative ARR growth, Firefly monetization, pricing strategy, executive appointments, and whether AI-first user growth eventually converts into higher-value subscriptions.

Investing.com -- S&P Global Ratings downgraded Salesforce Inc (NYSE:CRM) to 'A' from 'A+', pointing to an increasingly aggressive capital allocation strategy characterized by debt-funded shareholder returns and large-scale acquisitions. The ratings agency highlighted that recent dealmaking, alongside a $25 billion debt-financed share repurchase program, has pushed pro forma net debt-to-EBITDA above its previous 2x downgrade threshold.
The rating action reflects mounting risks that leverage could climb further as the enterprise software maker pursues an ambitious long-term expansion blueprint. S&P expects management will prioritize growth investments and buybacks over balance-sheet cash accumulation to reach its goal of expanding revenue from approximately $44 billion today to more than $63 billion by 2030.
That expansion push has already catalyzed significant deal activity, including pending or completed takeovers of Informatica for $9.5 billion, Braze for $5.7 billion, and Fin for $3.6 billion. S&P noted that Salesforce's organic revenue momentum has moderated, leaving the company increasingly reliant on programmatic M&A to generate 3 to 4 percentage points of its projected 11% fiscal 2027 top-line growth.
Near-term execution across core subscription operations remains solid, anchored by a 14% year-over-year lift in remaining performance obligations during the second quarter. While growth across the company's marketing and commerce offerings has softened recently, S&P indicated the Braze transaction could help reverse that trend and reinforce cross-selling momentum.
Longer term, Salesforce is directing resources toward monetizing its Data360 and Agentforce frameworks, which generated $3.9 billion in annual recurring revenue in the second quarter. Strong adoption of agentic AI offerings could lift customer spending by 1.5x to 2.0x and mitigate seat attrition risks, though the agency cautioned that material top-line contributions are unlikely over the next two fiscal years.
S&P assigned a stable outlook to the revised rating, projecting that strong free operating cash flow will allow Salesforce to sustain net leverage below 2.5x while defending its enterprise footprint. The agency warned, however, that further debt-funded buybacks, larger transactions pushing leverage beyond 2.5x, or disruptive AI competition could trigger additional downward rating pressure.

The surge is straining IT departments, with staff working overnight to patch software vulnerabilities, prompting some companies to turn to and increase investment in AI-powered security tools to help manage the workload.
A cyberattack on European supermarkets on Monday, the second in three weeks in which hackers raised refrigerator and freezer temperatures, forcing retailers to discard millions of dollars’ worth of spoiled food, underscored the urgency.

“We shut down one route, and before we’ve even finished rolling out the fix, the bad guys have moved on to the next,” she said, adding that hundreds of engineers at the company were now building AI-powered defense systems.
Nearly 37,000 security flaws in software or computer systems were reported in the third quarter of 2026, tripling from a year earlier, according to the Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures list, an international registry of disclosed security flaws.

Ionos said it changed its security practices after seeing a spike in vulnerabilities in July, deploying AI-based monitoring systems to scan for threats and using AI-assisted tools to install patches on its systems around the clock.
“I’m kind of limited to what a nine-to-five office hours team can do and that’s no longer good enough,” Noga said.

“AI also helps us to detect and to restore in a much faster way than we were ever able to do in the past,” she added.

European airlines suffered a second wave of bomb threats on Thursday that indiscriminately targeted companies from low-cost operator Wizz Air Holdings Plc to Finnish flag carrier Finnair Oyj, throwing air travel into disarray across a region already grappling with a series of security scares.
Among the flights affected was Aer Lingus Flight EI402 headed from Dublin to Rome, which was forced to make an emergency diversion to a military airfield in northern France. Finnair said two flights headed from Helsinki to Rome and Vienna got similar threats that turned out to be false.
Other carriers targeted included LOT Polish Airlines and Wizz, which was already at the receiving end of several threats earlier in the week. In the Czech Republic, police said they received bomb threats about four planes headed to Prague, and that the aircraft were searched after they touched down. Vienna’s main airport also received a warning about four flights, public broadcaster OFR reported.
Three Ryanair Holdings Plc flights headed to Sofia in Bulgaria from Madrid, Copenhagen and London were also targeted, a spokesperson for the Bulgarian ministry of transport said. Bulgarian MiG-29 fighter jets escorted the aircraft over Bulgaria’s airspace, the defense ministry said in a statement, and one of the flights was diverted to the city of Plovdiv.
Ryanair didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.

Missouri’s CAFO policy is built to multiply pollution, not prevent it
(Photo by Kent Becker, U.S. Geological Survey)
Missouri’s refusal to establish setback spacing requirements between concentrated animal feeding operations, to CAFOs. isn’t just a bureaucratic oversight — it’s a structural failure that guarantees cumulative pollution.
Our laws treat each CAFO as if it exists in isolation, but rural communities live with the reality of multiple industrial barns clustered together, all potentially draining into the same creeks, the same wells, and the same air column.
A single large CAFO can produce more manure than a small city. When two or three facilities operate side by side with no spacing requirements whatsoever, their waste streams can overlap. Yet the state reviews each permit separately instead of asking the obvious question: What happens when all that waste enters the same watershed? Rural Missouri already shows the consequences: increasing nitrate levels in private wells, persistent phosphorus pollution in streams, and industrial odors so strong that nearby residents cannot open their windows.
Missouri’s list of impaired waters has grown from 24 streams in 2002 to 549 in 2026. Of these, 215 were added after local control was removed in 2020 by SB391. Nearly half are impaired by e-coli or nutrients, potentially linked to CAFO waste and runoff.
The absence of setbacks is a likely accelerant. It allows industrial barns to stack like freight containers, concentrating millions of gallons of manure and wastewater in tight clusters. Regulators may insist each facility “meets its permit,” but permits don’t account for the combined load of multiple CAFOs operating in the same drainage area. Rural residents aren’t living next to one operation: they’re living next to the accumulated waste of an entire cluster.
A new trend is making the problem even worse: CAFOs are deliberately building barns just under the permit threshold to avoid regulation altogether. By staying a few animals below the number that triggers a state operation permit, operators side-step engineering reviews, public notice requirements, and even basic environmental safeguards. These “permit‑exempt” barns still produce enormous quantities of manure, yet they operate with virtually no oversight.
This loophole has become a strategy. Instead of one fully regulated barn, companies build two or three unregulated barns — each technically below the threshold but collectively producing the same waste load as a major CAFO. And because Missouri has no setbacks for Class II operations, these barns can be placed right next to each other, creating a de facto industrial complex with none of the protections that would normally apply.
The problem doesn’t stop at the property line. Missouri also refuses to regulate exported chicken litter — the waste hauled off‑site and spread on fields miles away. This creates a second layer of cumulative impact. A CAFO can legally export thousands of tons of manure into a watershed already saturated by neighboring operations, and regulators will still claim “no violation” because each facility’s paperwork looks clean.
This is the core failure: Missouri regulates CAFOs as isolated units, but pollution behaves as a single, combined system. Without setbacks, without spacing, without limits on exported waste, and without closing the permit‑exempt barn loophole, the cumulative burden grows heavier every year.

In his season-ending press conference, Cardinals president of baseball operations Chaim Bloom addressed several topics, from the team’s coaching staff to whether it will add pitching in the offseason to the progress of many of the team’s rookies this past season. But he created perhaps the most intrigue with his description of the team’s situation at third base, which he described as being a “long-term vacancy.”
Much of the Cardinals’ lineup looks mostly set for 2027, at least for now:
C: Leo Bernal
1B: Alec Burleson
2B: JJ Wetherholt
SS: Masyn Winn
LF: Joshua Baez
RF: Jordan Walker
DH: Ivan Herrera
That leaves center field and, yes, third base. So, with free agency now underway and the non-tender deadline looming on Nov. 20, here’s a look at five potential options for the Cardinals at third base for 2027.
The former top prospect: Nolan Gorman
This is probably the least likely name on the list. Given one more chance to win the third base job that was once thought to be his for the foreseeable future, Gorman struggled mightily in 2026, hitting .184 with just nine homers in 85 games. He was sent down to the Minors in June and stayed for two months to work on his swing, but he didn’t look appreciably better upon returning in late August, posting a .523 OPS in 73 plate appearances.
Gorman was a first-round pick by the Cardinals in 2018, and he’s been with the club for parts of five seasons, so he’s now due for a raise via arbitration in 2027. If the Cardinals can’t find a suitor willing to buy low on him, they could choose to non-tender Gorman, cutting him loose rather than offering him a contract for 2027. But the power stroke is still real, and this is a guy who had 27 homers as recently as 2023 … so maybe they give him one more chance?
The rookie: Blaze Jordan
Jordan was the player who was called up in June when Gorman was sent down, which was considered a surprise at the time because it was thought that Jordan wasn’t a good enough fielder to hold down third base on a regular basis. It turned out his defense was perfectly adequate, but the bat did not play as hoped. Jordan posted a .276 OBP, with only three homers and seven walks in 58 games.
That was a bit of a disappointment, considering he had a robust .921 OPS at Triple-A Memphis when he was called up. However, Jordan had been hitting a little better when he sustained a season-ending high ankle sprain on Aug. 27. Bloom, who drafted Jordan when he was with the Red Sox, clearly believes in him, and if Jordan is healthy, he might be the path of least resistance in the short term. But he’s going to have to hit a lot better if he wants to hold onto that job for long.
The utility guy: Thomas Saggese
Saggese got off to a very rough start in 2026 and was batting .184 when he was sent down in June. But when Jordan was injured in August, it was Saggese, not Gorman, who took advantage. He hit .279 with three homers and a .755 OPS over his final 25 games, which stood head and shoulders above anything else the Cardinals got at the position in 2026. He feels like a placeholder here -- one who could end up moving around the infield in a utility role -- but then again, he was a regular .300 hitter in the Minors and impressed many around the Cardinals in September.
It should be noted that Sagesse could have some competition even for that utility role.

Confluent, a subsidiary of IBM, has expanded its data streaming offerings with new functions aimed at supporting AI systems with real-time business context.
The company has made its Lightning Tables feature generally available on Amazon Web Services (AWS), finalising what it calls a five-pillar Data Streaming Platform (DSP).
Access deeper industry intelligence
Experience unmatched clarity with a single platform that combines unique data, AI, and human expertise.
This step adds query functionality to the existing capabilities to stream, connect, process and govern data under a unified approach for what Confluent terms the Streamhouse architecture.
The Streamhouse is intended to address a recurring challenge: as AI agents are introduced throughout enterprises, they must often make decisions based on fragmented, asynchronously updated data from a variety of systems.
This can result in decisions being made on outdated or conflicting information, potentially disrupting workflows.
The Streamhouse aims to resolve this by enabling the continuous capture, processing, governance and provision of current business information across systems, applications and analytics tools.
Confluent has illustrated the potential use case of an airline managing flight operations, where multiple systems can offer inconsistent views of aircraft locations, schedules and seat availability.
The Streamhouse model is designed to provide a constantly updated, shared view, allowing operational teams and AI decision-makers to respond in a timely and coordinated manner.
The architecture of the Streamhouse is built around three principles: it maintains continuously updated business information, it is designed for high availability and reliability, and it operates without requiring all data to be physically consolidated beforehand.
Rather than replacing existing data warehouses and lakehouses, it adds a real-time operational layer to support decision-making and actions.
At the centre of Confluent’s Data Streaming Platform is Apache Kafka, which streams business events.
The platform includes more than 150 managed and custom connectors for integrating enterprise data, batch execution features with Apache Flink, and tools for security and data governance such as schema and access policy controls.
The new query function offers several interfaces, including Confluent Tableflow for analytics, a Real-Time Context Engine for AI agents, and Lightning Tables for rapid SQL or API-based queries.
According to the company, Lightning Tables provides a read-only serving layer for data captured in Apache Kafka, enabling queries with reported latency between 10ms and 100ms and throughput exceeding 1,000 queries per second.
Features include multiple query interfaces, unified data governance, schema management and a machine learning feature store.
IBM Confluent and data general manager Shaun Clowes said: “The next era of enterprise AI will be won by the agents that know what’s happening in the business the moment they act. That’s what a Streamhouse can deliver.

Alphabet spent $160 billion on buildings and equipment over the last twelve months, compared with $28.8 billion in the twelve months to September 2023. So what share of Alphabet’s sales do you think goes to that bill today?
How Big Is Alphabet’s Spending Bill?
That spending consumed 33.9% of Alphabet’s sales over the last twelve months, up from 9.7% in the twelve months to September 2023. In dollars, the bill is about 5.5 times as large as it was three years ago. And it is still growing: Alphabet spent 114.4% more in the quarter to September 2026 than it did in the same quarter a year earlier.
Can Alphabet Pay For It?
Alphabet spent more on buildings and equipment than its business brought in as cash in the quarter to September 2026. In the same quarter a year earlier, that spending took only 49.5% of that cash.
Each row is one fiscal quarter. Cash left over is the cash the business brought in minus the spending (free cash flow). The spending leaves out equipment taken on through leases.
The cash left over after this spending went from a surplus to a shortfall, and it fell below zero in two of the last four quarters. Management said an inventory build for TPU system sales also held back cash in the latest quarter. Paying a 2018 fine in that quarter did as well. Even so, the business did not cover the bill on its own in the latest quarter.
Over the last twelve months, the business did still cover the bill. Spending stood at 89.0% of the cash the business brought in, but only because the quarters to December 2025 and March 2026 generated spare cash. Alphabet also ended September with $265 billion in cash and short-term investments, compared with $142 billion of debt. That cash includes $90.4 billion of stock Alphabet holds in other companies, and its debt was $33.7 billion a year earlier.
What Has The Spending Bought So Far?
Alphabet’s twelve-month sales grew 58.5% over the three years to September 2026. The company spent $287 billion on buildings and equipment during that time, and its business now brings in $73.1 billion more cash a year than it did then.
At that rate, it would take Alphabet about 3.9 years of the extra cash to earn back what it spent, though the spending is not the only reason the business brings in more. Alphabet does not yet have more cash left over to show for it: the cash left after the spending over the last twelve months was 74.6% lower than it was three years earlier.

Alphabet needs the long-term demand it sees for Google Cloud to show up as sales and cash. State officials aren’t requesting more money for next year and say they’ll resume processing applications only when monthly spending consistently falls below budget
Children play at Kids in Christ Academy in Kansas City with teacher Heather Malone on Oct. 23 (Steph Quinn/Missouri Independent).
Missouri childcare providers have classrooms sitting empty and parents eager to fill them. But with funding stretched thin, the state isn’t approving most new applications for subsidies that would make those openings affordable.
There were 11,618 children on the waiting list for Missouri’s childcare subsidy program on Oct. 5 — more than a third of all children eligible for assistance — according to the Department of Elementary and Secondary Education.
The department established the waiting list after demand increased by 19% between January 2025 and late February, exceeding the amount of money appropriated for fiscal year 2026.
No children have been moved off the list since it started March 1.
The program helps cover the cost of childcare for families earning no more than 150% of the federal poverty level. That’s $40,980 for a family of three, or the equivalent of one person earning $19.70 per hour for a year of full-time work. Families are responsible for paying a sliding scale rate based on their monthly income.
The average annual cost of childcare for an infant in Missouri is $13,780, according to Child Care Aware of Missouri. For a 4-year-old, it’s $9,568.
For families on the waiting list, that means finding a way to pay for care themselves — or going without it.
Christina Puckett, owner of Kids in Christ Academy in Kansas City, which serves 84 children ages six months through preschool, told The Independent she tries to help when she can.
Even before the waitlist, Puckett said, some families receiving subsidies struggled to pay their sliding scale rate.
“The struggle was there before the waiting list,” Puckett said.
Now families ask Puckett if they can enroll their children at Kids in Christ and pay out of pocket until the department begins processing applications on the waiting list.
Puckett said she gives discounts “just to help some parents because they can’t afford that.”
“I have them text me, ‘Can I bring my kid in? I just want to pay you,’” Puckett said. “Well, I know they can’t afford to pay me, so then what do I do?”
Despite the growing waiting list, the department is not requesting additional funding for the program in fiscal year 2028.

Modern life has made movement optional like never before. ASICS research found that respondents around the world reported spending 86 percent of their waking day not moving. Yet our bodies were shaped by a very different world, where walking, carrying, and running were part of everyday survival.
Around two million years ago, our ancestors began developing a body equipped for endurance running. These adaptations helped them keep moving over long distances. We inherited that capacity, but modern life gives many of us little reason to use it.
A marathon puts that evolutionary inheritance to the test, with modern training, nutrition, and technology helping runners explore their limits. So how would we perform lined up against the ancestors who helped shape us? Could a recreational marathoner outrun Homo erectus?
Evolution Toward Endurance
Unlike other mammals, “humans aren’t especially good sprinters, but we are highly effective endurance athletes,” says David Raichlen, an evolutionary biologist at the University of Southern California.
Some two million years ago, our ancestors Homo erectus lived as hunter-gatherers, spending long periods walking, tracking, and chasing food. “Around the same time, they began to develop some anatomical features that improved their ability to run for long periods,” Raichlen says. “These features include long legs, relatively short toes, long Achilles tendons, a large gluteus maximus, and other traits that help to stabilize the head and trunk while running.”
Our ability to sweat profusely may also have given early humans an advantage in hot conditions, allowing them to cool down and keep moving while other animals overheated.
One popular explanation is persistence hunting: chasing prey over hours until it collapses from heat exhaustion. Professor Lewis Halsey, of the University of Roehampton, says the evidence has become more nuanced. His own research comparing humans and horses supports a human heat-endurance advantage. Humans are less adversely affected by rising temperatures than horses, although horses remain faster. Human success, he suggests, may have come from combining a modest heat advantage with pacing, tracking, cooperation, and a large brain for tactics.
The Marathon Question
Some internet speculations suggest Homo erectus could run a marathon in around 3 to 4 hours. If the estimate were taken at face value, even its slower end would beat today’s average marathon time of around 4:30 (4:17:00 for men and 4:43:00 for women, according to Running USA’s Industry Insights report from 2023). But where did the Homo erectus marathon time come from?
It remains unclear. One study, focused on time rather than speed and published in the 2020 Journal of Human Evolution, offers a different measure of endurance: its model estimated that Homo erectus would reach a dehydration limit after 5.5-5.7 hours of persistence hunting without drinking, under the conditions examined.
Raichlen cautions against putting a time on possible speed. “I would not say that we know Homo erectus ‘could run a 3:30 marathon’,” he says. “The stronger conclusion is that around two million years ago, humans had evolved a body capable of surprisingly impressive endurance running.”
Halsey is blunter. “Inferring a marathon time from some bones is pushing it,” he says. Many adaptations associated with running are also useful for walking, and they tell us nothing about VO2 max or lactate threshold—key determinants of distance-running

JPMorgan Chase & Co. NYSE: JPM is preparing for interest rates to move in either direction, but a rapid rise poses a broader risk to the financial system, according to Charles Bristow, the bank’s head of treasury and chief investment officer.
Bristow said the bank has stress-tested its balance sheet against higher rates and does not have a single “nightmare scenario.” His greater concern is that a sudden repricing could leave other institutions unable to adjust their balance sheets quickly, undermine confidence and trigger competition for funding.
“If the move to higher rates needs to be too fast, it will have very non-linear and unpredictable outcomes,” he said.
Rates and balance-sheet strategy
Bristow said the market was pricing just over two interest-rate hikes through the end of 2027, near what he considers the lower end of a credible range. While he said market pricing was not far off on a probability-weighted basis, he remained cautious about the risk of rates moving higher.
For JPMorgan’s investment portfolio, he said the more consequential question is where the market settles on the economy’s tendency toward inflation and the Federal Reserve’s neutral rate. Medium-term rate forwards have risen to around 5% from 3% about four years ago, he said, reflecting a shift toward an environment of higher growth, investment and inflation pressure.
The bank’s approach to managing the duration of its balance sheet has not fundamentally changed, Bristow said. JPMorgan has generally avoided longer-dated investments because it believed markets had underpriced a return to a period of substantial public- and private-sector infrastructure investment. He added that current pricing makes that position harder to maintain than it was four years ago.
He also said a proposed accounting change allowing hedging of held-to-maturity securities could give the bank room, at the margin, to take more interest-rate exposure in low-credit-risk instruments within that portfolio.
Buybacks, deposits and capital rules
Asked about a decline in third-quarter share repurchases, Bristow said the bank’s sustainable dividend is its primary capital-return commitment. Beyond that, JPMorgan weighs buybacks against potential uses of capital over the medium term.
He said growth in risk-weighted assets was running at approximately a double-digit compound annual rate and that the bank was already finding organic opportunities to deploy capital. Retaining capital for future opportunities was prudent, he said, given the bank’s cost of capital and demand for financing.
On deposits, Bristow said customers have had considerable time to seek higher rates since the 2022–2023 cycle. Both consumer giants beat earnings, yet their margins are moving in opposite directions as oil prices climb and a cautious U.S. shopper holds back. One dividend carries a thin balance sheet buffer, and retirees need to know which one.

Procter & Gamble (NYSE:PG | PG Price Prediction) and Colgate-Palmolive (NYSE:CL) reported eight days apart, and both beat revenue and earnings expectations. For retirees, the key question is which dividend can absorb oil-driven cost spikes, currency swings, and a hesitant U.S. shopper? The two companies answered it differently.
Shoppers Buy More P&G Products While Colgate Wins on Price
P&G posted Q1 FY2027 core EPS of $2.00, beating the $1.89 estimate. Organic sales rose 4.0%, and volume supplied 2.4 points of that gain. That points to more households buying Tide and Pampers, which is the soundest kind of growth. Pampers Amore alone is projected to exceed $100 million in first-year sales. The cost is margin: core gross margin fell 150 basis points, and management sees a $1.4 billion after-tax commodity pressure that assumes $100 Brent crude. As management put it, “The strength is real, but it won’t be a straight line.”
Colgate beat with base EPS of $0.97 against a $0.93 estimate. Pricing drove 2.0% of its 3.6% organic growth, and base gross margin expanded 90 bps to 60.3%. That margin direction runs opposite to P&G’s. North America remains a soft spot, with volume down 3.7%. CEO Noel Wallace called the U.S. fix “very much a work in progress.”
Cash Coverage Exposes a Balance Sheet Gap
P&G’s forward dividend equals roughly 62% of its $7.00 core EPS guidance midpoint. That leaves comfortable room. FY2026 free cash flow of $15.84B covers the planned $10B-plus in dividends, with buybacks absorbing most of the rest.
Colgate grew free cash flow 7%, yet shareholders’ equity fell to $288M after years of repurchases. I see that thin buffer as a real constraint. Currency adds risk too: FX lifted Latin America sales by 6.5%, but Brazil’s real has since turned against the dollar.
Investors have rewarded Colgate’s margin story anyway. Its shares are up 29.3% year to date versus 21.33% for P&G.
Oil and U.S. Market Share Will Settle This in 2027
I’m watching whether P&G’s pricing-with-innovation approach holds as greater cost pressure arrives in the back half. Management wants more than 80% of its top U.S. customers holding or growing share by year-end. For Colgate, keep an eye on the 2027 U.S. innovation cycle. Wallace already warned, “We do not see the headwinds on commodities lightening up as we exit the year.”
Why P&G’s Dividend Looks Sturdier for Retirement Income
For income-focused investors considering these names, P&G offers a higher yield, a bigger recent raise, a longer run, and cash flow that covers the payout well even with core EPS guidance flat to slightly up. Colgate fits a dividend-growth investor who can stomach emerging-market currency swings for its expanding margins and Hill’s momentum. Salesforce (NYSE:CRM | CRM Price Prediction) and ServiceNow (NYSE:NOW) both reported recently and made the same pitch: agentic AI will power their next phase of growth. Investors have pushed back since. ServiceNow fell 27.58% over the past week, and Salesforce slipped 6.17%. The businesses below look stronger than either move suggests.
Agentforce Lifts Salesforce While One Guide Spooks ServiceNow Holders
Salesforce posted Q2 revenue of $11.345B, up 10.8%. That pace is steady but modest. The AI layer is growing much faster. Combined Agentforce and Data 360 ARR reached nearly $3.9B, up over 210%, and 50% of Agentforce bookings came from customers buying more credits. That tells me customers keep using agents after they go live. Marc Benioff said “We’re seeing incredible demand for our AI and data products, with ARR about to cross $4 billion.”
ServiceNow grew subscription revenue 21% to $3.988B, which is faster than Salesforce. It also raised its 2026 AI net new ACV target for the second time this year, to $1.7B. Still, non-GAAP EPS of $1.00 came in below the $1.02 estimate, and the Q4 cRPO guide slowed to 18.5%. Management blamed early renewals and public-sector deals that run on customers’ own servers. That explanation sounds reasonable, but I want to see it confirmed.
Data Keeper Versus Agent Governor
Salesforce argues that AI makes its customer data more valuable. Legora’s CFO put it simply: “the agent is only as good as the context that you give it.” With Headless 360, customers can work with Salesforce data inside Slack, ChatGPT, or Teams, so Salesforce gets paid whichever chat tool wins.
ServiceNow wants to manage every AI agent a company runs. AI Passport gives each agent a record of what it can access, which management called “the most capable kill switch available in the enterprise today.” Through its Action Fabric tool, work that starts in ChatGPT still runs, and earns money, inside ServiceNow.
Capital allocation separates the two companies. Salesforce’s $25B buyback cut diluted shares to 821M from 962M. ServiceNow’s acquisitions shrank its GAAP operating margin to 9.5% from 17%, a real cost of buying growth.
Premium Upgrades and Q4 Backlog Decide the Next Move
Salesforce’s push to move customers onto premium editions will be worth watching. Only 5% of sales and service users have upgraded, and those tiers cost 60% to 80% more. That leaves plenty of room to grow. For ServiceNow, keep an eye on whether Q4 cRPO meets the guide. Bill McDermott said the “true acceleration” arrives in 2027.
Why I Trust Both, for Different Reasons
On valuation metrics, Salesforce screens as the cheaper of the two. A forward P/E of 14 and a big buyback limit the downside. ServiceNow screens as the faster grower. A 98% renewal rate shows customers stick around, and the selloff lowers the price investors pay for that growth. The U.S. economy isn't expected to have produced much job growth in October, with employers reluctant to hire workers but also not cutting staff amid a shrinking labor force and a growing problem of long-term unemployment.
Economists are looking for a meager nonfarm payrolls gain of 59,000, a slight uptick from the 29,000 jobs produced in September, according to the Dow Jones consensus. That result would continue a pattern of sparse growth.

Evaluating the health of the labor market in such a climate becomes a moving target, Bachaud said.
More clues will come Friday when the Bureau of Labor Statistics releases the October nonfarm payrolls report at 8:30 a.m. ET.

The 23-year-old from Easton, Pennsylvania, showed up to the starting line in Staten Island dressed as a hot dog and finished in 2:49:15, which, after hearing, made me think I could’ve done a lot more than just iron my name onto my tank top.
Pezzino, a personal trainer and group fitness coach, was attempting to break a Guinness World Record for the fastest marathon dressed as a savory food. Guinness still has to review the evidence before anything becomes official, but judging by the number of people who noticed her on Sunday, finding witnesses won't be a problem.
When speaking with Runner’s World, Pezzino said the hot dog wasn't even originally part of her marathon plans—and neither, for a while, was running another marathon at all.
Pezzino had been competing since childhood, starting in a local running series at age 4 before moving on to cross country and track in high school and college. She made her marathon debut in Chicago in 2024. She returned the following year, but a serious medical emergency at Mile 17 forced her to drop out. Afterward, she strongly considered giving up running altogether.
"I'd put too much pressure on myself and lost the joy in the sport," she told Runner's World.

With any luck, doing this would be a chance to enjoy running again without making every race about the clock.

She lost her mother to a rare cancer in 2022, and Mike, the husband of a close family friend, died from multiple myeloma. She had partnered with MMRF for her first marathon and wanted to reconnect with the organization. “If successfully exploited, the actors could change the temperature and possibly cause physical impacts such as fire hazards, loss of inventory and changes to the service life of the system,” said the statement, which was jointly issued by the FBI, the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency and the departments of health, transport and agriculture.
“Every organization that depends on refrigeration and monitoring systems should assume it could be a target,” said Chris Butera, CISA’s acting executive assistant director for cybersecurity.
FBI Cyber Branch Operations Director Brett Leatherman said that the government was “seeing these systems targeted across critical infrastructure sectors globally.”
The government urged operators of industrial refrigeration control systems to pull their devices off the public internet, isolate them from their corporate networks and promptly apply software updates.
At least three waves of hacks have hit commercial fridges and freezers in the past few months. Pentagon investigators are treating a series of mysterious malfunctions that hit grocery store refrigeration units on US military bases in August as a cyberattack, Reuters first reported last week. A sweeping hack of French freezers last month dealt tens of millions of euros’ worth of damage, while a second wave of hacking affected more than 100 stores across Europe on Monday.
The hacks have raised concerns over the ability of hackers to remotely tamper with refrigerators and other critical devices.

Parents in North Carolina sued Google after their 13-year-old daughter spent months discussing suicidal thoughts with the company’s artificial intelligence tools on her school-issued Chromebook, underscoring the potential risks of the technology as parents and educators debate AI’s place in schools.
The girl exchanged thousands of messages with Google’s flagship AI model, Gemini, many of which detailed anxiety, depression and methods of committing suicide, according to the complaint, filed in California state court. By the time the school notified her parents, she had been corresponding with Google about such topics for months, often using a feature in Google Search known as AI Mode. The complaint alleges that as Google infuses more AI into its products for schools, the company is exposing students to dangerous technology without giving parents and administrators fair warning.
“In marketing inherently dangerous Chromebooks as safe and sneaking Gemini into them to gain on its competition, Google exploited its trusted position in K-12 education for its own commercial benefit,” the family’s lawyers, Julie and Andrew Liddell, write in the lawsuit, referring to Google’s flagship AI model, known as Gemini. Chromebooks are a low-cost laptop from Google that have become the dominant device for students in the US. “Google must be held to account for treating the lives of children as disposable in service of its bottom line.”
Google didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.
Over the past few years, Google has spent billions of dollars to compete in the race to build powerful AI models. One edge Google has over rivals such as startups Anthropic PBC and OpenAI is its prominent place in schools, putting the company’s technology in front of students as they form technological habits for life. Google’s Chrome operating system ran on 58% of the tablets shipped last year to K-12 schools, compared with Microsoft Corp.’s 22%, according to Futuresource Consulting.
Amid a torrent of criticism from parents and schools, Google moved this week to turn AI tools, including Google Search, off by default for K-12 student accounts. But the change came with a catch: Schools that turn Google Search back on will have to accept the AI features that come with it. Google has said the move is an attempt to give schools more control, pointing to the release of a new search feature called Guided Learning, which unpacks how to solve a problem rather than just serving up the answer.

Pittsburgh’s Allegheny County passed one of the nation’s most generous parental leave mandates last month, putting businesses there on the hook for as much as 12 weeks of a worker’s full salary.
After Tuesday’s elections, employers around the country have reason to pay attention.
Democratic gains in Congress and statehouses are giving new momentum to paid leave and expanded child care, issues that featured prominently in political campaigns this year. Incoming governors in Wisconsin and Georgia ran on expanding early childhood education, while voters in Marin County, California, are on track to pass a tax increase that may raise up to $12.5 million a year to help more families afford child care.
For businesses, the question isn’t just whether those policies will advance, but how they’ll work and who will pay.
Allegheny County offers a glimpse of what’s at stake. Its new rule requires companies with at least 15 employees to provide 12 weeks of parental leave at full pay after the birth, adoption, stillbirth or placement of a child, capped at $4,200 per week. Unlike state paid-leave programs that spread costs through centralized insurance systems funded by taxes on workers and businesses, Allegheny leaves employers responsible for covering the benefits themselves.
That has alarmed many Pittsburgh-area small businesses and nonprofits. Many worry they’ll have to reduce hiring or cut services in order to comply.
“Having time available for parents to spend with their kids is important for us, but the challenge was that the full burden of this policy was put on the business,” said Mark Heinbockel, the executive director of mental-health charity Anchorpoint Counseling Ministry in McCandless Township. He said his organization may have to scale back services when an employee is on parental leave.
Len Semplice, the owner of Redbeard’s Sports Bar & Grill in Pittsburgh, said he believes in parental-leave policies, especially at large companies, and is open to plans overseen by the government. He said he’s considering raising prices to preserve an already slim profit margin. “I’m going to have to charge someone to make up the difference. It goes to the consumer in a way,” he added.
He also worries people will take advantage of the policy, working the bare minimum — six months or 625 hours — to qualify for the benefit and then not return after the leave period ends. “What guarantees they’re coming back?” Semplice asked.
Nonprofits that advocated both for and against the plan estimated the policy may cost employers between $170 million to $300 million, given projections that roughly 2% of the county’s workers might use it in a given year.
The fight may already be overtaken by Tuesday’s election. Democrats won control of Pennsylvania’s state Senate, giving the party control of both chambers and the governor’s office. That may revive a statewide paid-leave policy that passed the Democrat-controlled House this year and stalled in the Republican-led Senate. The state proposal would spread the cost through a payroll deduction-funded insurance system that could supersede the Pittsburgh-area plan.

Google, Meta Platforms and TikTok sued California to block enforcement of a new state law intended to limit the risk of addicting children under age 16 to online platforms.
The law, known as Assembly Bill 1709, prohibits those platforms from offering underage children “psychologically exploitative features” that could lead to compulsive use, such as providing personal recommendations and sending videos through autoplay features. It also requires the deletion of children’s accounts with those features.
In separate lawsuits on Wednesday, Google, Meta and TikTok said the law wrongly compels them to honor the state’s preferred means of presenting content to children, and substitutes the state’s judgment for that of parents. They said the law violates the US Constitution’s First Amendment’s free speech protections, as well as Section 230 of the federal Communications Decency Act, which broadly shields online platforms from liability over user content.
Related: Snap Finalizing Settlement to Avoid LA Trial on Addiction Claims
“The state cannot, consistent with the First Amendment, override Meta’s editorial judgments about how to curate and display … billions of posts of third-party speech,” the Facebook and Instagram parent said in its complaint. Google, which owns YouTube and is a unit of Alphabet, and TikTok, a unit of China’s ByteDance, made similar arguments.
The office of California Attorney General Rob Bonta, who enforces the state’s laws and is the only defendant, did not immediately respond on Thursday to requests for comment.
Governor Gavin Newsom signed the law on September 10. He said children’s safety should be central to any discussion about technology, and California “will not stand by while unregulated technology puts our children at risk.”
Thousands of Lawsuits Allege Addiction
Some critics accused California of overreaching by restricting children’s online access. The Electronic Frontier Foundation, a nonprofit digital rights advocacy group, called the law “a massive privacy and free speech nightmare.”
Many U.S. states regulate children’s access to social media. Countries around the world have similar restrictions, including a ban in Australia on social media for children under 16.
Related: As AI Laws Proliferate, Liability and Coverage Questions Multiply
In August, Meta agreed to pay up to $18 billion and limit teenagers’ use of Facebook and Instagram under agreements with nearly all U.S. states, which accused it of violating privacy and consumer protection laws.
Google filed its lawsuit in federal court in San Jose, California. Meta sued in San Francisco, and TikTok sued in Los Angeles.
The companies and Snapchat parent Snap SNAP.N still face thousands of lawsuits by individuals, school districts, municipalities and other government entities claiming they sought to addict children and caused a mental health crisis that resulted in such harms as anxiety, depression and suicide.

The next stop in Allstate’s journey with artificial intelligence – a personal agentic assistant for consumers.
CEO Tom Wilson revealed that customers could expect an Allstate PAA early in 2027. He said the PAA has been in development for more than a year.
“The foundational technology is in place…the algorithms are being tested,” he said.
Related: Allstate Q3 Net Income Drops About 45% on Higher Catastrophe Losses
“We want to give customers more value every day in as many ways as we can, including leveraging technology, and having a PAA will enable more people to come to us,” Wilson said during an earnings with analysts. “If they don’t feel like calling an Allstate agent – or feel like getting on our website – and they just want to have a PAA do that, we’re fine with that.”
Wilson said personal lines new business is up 125% over 2019, and currently split about eventually between exclusive agents, independent agents, and direct-to-consumer. However, the advent of PAAs “gives us the opportunity to serve consumers who prefer to have a machine to handle their transactions,” Wilson added.
Allstate said it does not yet have a name for its PAA, but it will leverage Allstate’s Large Language Intelligent Ecosystem (ALLIE), which is ingesting code at a much high rate than just a few months ago. The insurer has already launched a customer service agent called Ask Allstate, which handles a variety of inquiries for customers.
Allstate said its PAA will also work with existing PAAs, such as Muse.
Related: Allstate Introduces Large Language Model, ALLIE
“Essentially, we’re now marketing to machines and people, not just marketing to people,” Wilson explained. “These capabilities also give us the opportunity to be offensive in leveraging capabilities by launching a PAA that’s an expert in protection that still meets consumers’ needs and their desires for fewer clicks.”
The PAA will additionally provide context on coverage needs of the customer, he added.
Wilson said the speed of the development of this market is unclear, but getting in now “will enable Allstate to provide increased value for customers.”
“We believe that this will actually help the existing PAAs out there,” Wilson said. When asked about possible regulatory or cyber concerns, Wilson added that Allstate will “figure out stuff like what do we do with the regulators, what do we do with privacy, what do we do with cybersecurity, as we go.”
“There’s work to be done, but the benefit to customers and the economic rationale is going to move this train down the path,” Wilson said. “This is going to happen. So we decided to get in on it, accelerate it, go as fast as we can, which is why we started leaning into the PAA.”
